questions.q: If you have a square with a side length of 3 cm, what is its area and what is the unit used to express it?
questions.a: The area is 9 cm². A student who says "12 cm" is confusing area with perimeter (adding sides instead of multiplying), and one who says "9 cm" has forgotten that area units must be "square" (cm²).

questions.q: Explain in your own words why we use "square units" instead of just "units" to measure area.
questions.a: We use square units because we are counting how many 1x1 unit squares fit inside the shape. A student who says "because it is standard" doesn't understand the geometry behind the measurement.

questions.q: A rectangular floor is 6 meters long and 4 meters wide. How many square-meter tiles are needed to cover the entire floor?
questions.a: 6 m × 4 m = 24 square meters. If the student adds 6 + 4, they are incorrectly calculating the perimeter instead of the area.

questions.q: If you double the length of a rectangle while keeping the width the same, what happens to the area?
questions.a: The area doubles. A student saying it stays the same or triples is not visualizing the relationship between the dimensions (Area = l × w).

questions.q: Is it possible for two different rectangles to have the same area but different perimeters? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes. A 4x6 rectangle (Area 24, Perimeter 20) and a 3x8 rectangle (Area 24, Perimeter 22) prove this. A student saying "no" fails to realize that dimensions can change while their product remains constant.

questions.q: Create a problem where you have to calculate the "leftover" area of a garden after placing a swimming pool inside it. What information would you need?
questions.a: To solve this, I need the dimensions of the garden and the dimensions of the pool. A good answer includes a plan to subtract the pool's area from the total garden area; a poor answer ignores the need for both sets of dimensions.
